newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt's forces search for gunmen who massacred 13.
newsitem.headline: Egypt's forces search for gunmen who massacred 13.

text.p: Egyptian security forces on Friday set up roadblocks and combed sugar cane fields in the southern Qena province in an operation to hunt down suspected Moslem militants who massacred 13 people.

"It was a total surprise. We still don't know why it happened," a police officer told Reuters by telephone from Nag Hammadi town, near the hamlet of Ezbet Dawoud and about 450 km (280 miles) south of Cairo.

He said police were inspecting the scene of the shooting in Ezbet Dawoud, where 13 people were killed late on Thursday when gunmen opened fire at random on a crowded street before fleeing into sugar cane fields.
It was one of the bloodiest attacks since militants launched their anti-government campaign in 1992 to overthrow the government and turn Egypt into a strict Islamic state.

Hours after the first attack, gunmen opened fire on a train passing through Nag Hammadi on its way to Cairo from Aswan. Seven people were wounded in that attack and one woman later died of her injuries, the interior ministry said.
Security sources had put the number of wounded at 15.
The interior ministry said roadblocks were in place as security forces combed the area for the gunmen.
Security sources said they believed gunmen from the military wing of al-Gama'a al-Islamiyah (Islamic Group) were responsible for both attacks.
Witnesses in Ezbet Dawoud said the gunmen's rampage through the hamlet's main road lasted about 30 minutes.

Security sources said the gunmen, armed with automatic rifles, first opened fire at a tailor's shop, killing its owner and another man. They continued walking along the road, shooting at passersby before escaping in nearby fields, the sources said.
The people in Ezbet Dawoud are mainly Coptic Christians and a list of victim's names released by the ministry indicated that eight of the 12 people it said had died were Christians.
Their ages ranged from 20 to the mid-60s.
Egyptian police are still looking for five men they suspect of massacring 10 Coptic Christians in an attack on a church in Minya province last month.
The Gama'a has attacked several trains in southern Egypt in the past because they sometimes carry tourists, who had once been targets in the group's anti-government drive.
The group has also targetted ministers, policemen and Christians in its armed campaign.
More than 1,000 people have been killed in political violence since militants took up arms.
